title: The chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:1–14)
hook: Elisha won't leave Elijah and asks for a double portion of his spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naboth's vineyard, and a prophet who told a king, I have found thee. Your line was not for sale.

Two men are on the road out of Gilgal, an old prophet and his student. Elijah stops and says, "Tarry here, I pray thee." Stay here; the LORD has sent me on to Bethel. At Bethel, a company of prophets asks Elisha: don't you know the LORD will take your master from you today? His answer is short: "Yea, I know it; hold ye your peace." And Elijah says it again: tarry here. And again.

Three times Elijah tells him to stay behind: at Gilgal, at Bethel, at Jericho. Three times Elisha gives the same answer, in the King James words: "As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee." They walk on to the Jordan. Elijah takes his mantle, his cloak, rolls it up, and strikes the water, and it parts, and they cross on dry ground. Across the river, Elijah turns to him: "Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee." Elisha doesn't ask small: "I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me." Some readers hear an echo of the law in Deuteronomy, where the firstborn son receives a double portion: Elisha is asking to be his heir. Elijah is honest: "Thou hast asked a hard thing." But if you see me when I'm taken, it will be yours. As they walk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, "and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven." The text is exact here: the chariot parted them, and the whirlwind took him up. Elisha cries out, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof." He tears his own clothes in two. Then he picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah, walks back to the Jordan, and strikes the water with it, asking, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" The water parts. The one who wouldn't leave is the one left holding the mantle. He stayed to the end, he asked plainly, and he saw.
screen: `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE, THREE TIMES.`
`WHERE IS THE LORD GOD OF ELIJAH?`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you how to live, or work, or believe: a parent, a coach, a pastor. If they're still here, ask yourself what you'd want to ask of them, plainly, before it's too late; if they're gone, ask what mantle they left in your hands. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Mantle. Elijah's cloak, which parted the Jordan and then fell to Elisha, who refused to leave his teacher and asked for a double portion of his spirit.
Your line: I will not leave you. A week from a kingdom torn in two, through ravens, a widow's jar, Carmel, a broom tree and a stolen vineyard, to a chariot of fire. A full week.

howItsDone: Some Christians speak of 'passing the mantle' when one generation of leaders hands on to the next, and some churches echo Elisha's request for a double portion when they pray for new leaders.

original.note: Hebrew: a cloak or mantle; Elijah's mantle parts the Jordan, and then falls to Elisha (2 Kings 2:8, 2:13).

what a scholar hears: the text says Elijah went up by a whirlwind, the chariot parting them (2:11); some readers link the double portion to the firstborn's share (Deuteronomy 21:17).

chat.says: Why did Elisha keep refusing when Elijah told him to stay behind?
options: He was loyal to the end: I will not leave thee, three times.
He didn't trust Elijah and wanted to watch him the whole way.
He was lost and didn't know the road back from the Jordan.
chat.meaning: Three times Elisha answered, I will not leave thee; he stayed to the end, asked plainly, and was left holding the mantle.

notes: 'Three times' Elijah says tarry here: 2:2 (Gilgal), 2:4 (Bethel), 2:6 (Jericho), each answered with 'I will not leave thee'. Counted from the text.
'A company of prophets' renders the KJV 'sons of the prophets' (2:3, 2:5); the Jericho group is merged into the Bethel scene in the hook.
The double portion / firstborn link (Deuteronomy 21:17) is attributed to 'some readers'.
